meta.title: Who really said "When we are tired, we are attacked by ideas we conquered long ago"? | Quotle.info
meta.description: No source in Nietzsche's corpus, and — the giveaway — no German original exists. The German versions in circulation appear back-translated from the English. Earliest known printing: Rudolf Flesch's Book of Unusual Quotations, 1957.
meta.ogTitle: Who really said 'When we are tired, we are attacked by ideas we conquered long ago'?
meta.ogDescription: Not found in Nietzsche, and no German original exists — the German versions look back-translated from English. First printed in a 1957 quotation anthology, uncited.

answer.label: Not sourced to Nietzsche — origin unknown
answer.sourceLine: It appears in none of Nietzsche’s books or notebooks. The decisive detail is linguistic: no German original has ever been found, and the German versions circulating today appear to be back-translations from the English — the opposite of what you would expect from a German philosopher. Its earliest known printing is a 1957 quotation anthology, credited to him with no documentation.

source.excerpt: When we are tired, we are attacked by ideas we conquered long ago.
trail: No German original exists. Researchers looking for one found only German versions that appear to have been translated from the English — a strong indicator that the sentence was composed in English and later attributed backwards Quote Investigator ↗.

The earliest known printing is Rudolf Flesch’s The Book of Unusual Quotations (1957), crediting Nietzsche without documentation. It then passes through a 1958 newspaper, a 1962 column, the 1966 Viking Book of Aphorisms, and onward into standard reference works — every instance citation-free full chain ↗.
It does not appear on Wikiquote’s Nietzsche page at all — not among his sourced quotations, and not even in the disputed or misattributed lists Wikiquote ↗.
source.excerptNote: The sentence as first printed in 1957. Note that this English text is the earliest form known — there is no German behind it to translate from.
source.rightsNote: Effectively unattributable rather than reusable-with-credit. There is no known author and no known translator, so there is nobody to credit and no rights holder to clear; a sentence of this length would not attract copyright in the United States in any case. The honest way to use it is as an anonymous saying of unknown twentieth-century origin — not as Nietzsche. This is not legal advice.

author.name: Friedrich Nietzsche
author.heading: Why it gets pinned on Nietzsche
author.bio: Friedrich Nietzsche (1844–1900) wrote in aphorisms, which makes him uniquely easy to counterfeit: a single free-standing sentence about weakness, exhaustion and the return of discarded beliefs looks exactly like something from Beyond Good and Evil. He is one of the most quote-magnetized names in philosophy, and lines that merely sound Nietzschean are routinely absorbed into his corpus — this one entered it through a 1957 anthology.

misattribution.heading: The attribution problem
misattribution.intro: Most misattributions are hard to disprove. This one carries an unusually clean piece of negative evidence: the language itself.

items.why: Nietzsche wrote in German. If this were his, a German sentence would exist and be findable. None does — and the German versions in circulation look like back-translations from the English, which is what you get when an English sentence acquires a German author the finding ↗.
From the 1957 anthology onward — through newspapers, a 1966 aphorism collection, and later Oxford and Random House reference works — every printing credits him and none cites a work, section or year.
It does not appear among his sourced quotations, nor in the disputed or misattributed sections — it never acquired enough of a claim to argue about Wikiquote ↗.

misattribution.truthLine: Author unknown. No German original exists; the earliest known printing is a 1957 English-language anthology that credited Nietzsche without documentation full chain ↗.

context.heading: Why it resonates
lead: It describes something real and rarely named: convictions you thought you had settled come back when you are too depleted to argue with them. Anyone who has lain awake at three in the morning recognises it immediately.
It also sounds like late Nietzsche — the vocabulary of conquest and attack, the single-sentence form, the interest in what exhaustion reveals. Sounding right is how a sentence acquires an author.
detailsBody: 1957: Rudolf Flesch, The Book of Unusual Quotations — credited to Nietzsche, no source.
1958–1962: a Pennsylvania newspaper, then a syndicated columnist, repeat it.
1966: W. H. Auden and Louis Kronenberger, The Viking Book of Aphorisms.
Later: absorbed into Oxford and Random House quotation references — still with no citation.
Variant: ‘…we are assaulted by ideas we conquered long ago.’
context.pull: Nietzsche wrote in German. There is no German.
